sections.heading: How they personalized onboarding
sections.content: They initially used one generic guided onboarding, which they believed could address more than 90% of users’ needs, and personalized from that starting point. For segmentation, learning style and building style worked better than conventional categories such as marketing, product management, or operations, and produced better activation results. The team considered whether someone needed more database familiarity or a more visual rather than data-forward learning experience. It also added personalization to help users build something relevant to their use case, rather than something generic. Isford described gathering teammate-versus-builder information in the flow as a future idea for routing people to different experiences, not as an established feature.

sections.heading: What the guided experience looked like
sections.content: The wizard used easy-to-click questions—for example, what kind of project the person was working on and what they wanted to track—and visualized the workflow as they made choices. Isford said this reduced the effort and cognitive load of getting started with Airtable’s complicated product; she cautioned that the immersive wizard may be especially suited to products where getting started is challenging, rather than every product.

answer.summary: Lauryn Isford’s team used customer research and behavior patterns to identify differences in how people build and learn—not just their job titles—then used signup questions and onboarding personalization to better support those needs. They started with a generic guided onboarding flow designed to help more than 90% of users, and personalized from there.

sections.heading: How they identified user types
sections.content: They spoke with customers, watched them get started, and looked for patterns and clusters in behavior. A research team also conducted surveys and customer conversations outside the production experience, giving the team a read on different building and learning types before designing the flow. Signup questions could vary depending on what the team wanted to learn about a user.

sections.heading: How they grouped users and personalized
sections.content: They found it more effective to segment by learning style and building style than by conventional categories such as marketing, product management, or operations. For example, one user might need more familiarity with databases, while another might benefit from a more visual rather than data-forward learning experience. They tailored the experience to those needs; this approach produced better activation results than traditional segments. They initially offered a generic guided onboarding, which they felt addressed more than 90% of users’ needs, and then personalized from that starting point.

sections.heading: A possible further distinction
sections.content: Isford described collecting role-in-the-workflow information—such as whether someone was a teammate helping on a project rather than the person building it—as a future idea. She said that information could route people to a fully different experience; the passage presents this as a possibility, not as an implemented personalization.
